name: Theodora 'Teddy' Quayle
equipment: A dark green travelling dress, much mended, with a hidden pocket in the skirt and another in the sleeve
Derringer (Remington over-and-under, .41), 2 rounds loaded, in the sleeve pocket
Boot knife in her right boot
A faro box, a dealing layout rolled in oilcloth, a case keeper and a set of ivory checks, the tools of her new trade
Two decks of playing cards, one honest and one less so
A telegrapher's key and sounder in a wooden box, her own, which she takes everywhere and cannot explain why
A railroad pass on the River Line, revoked in May, which nobody has yet asked her to give back
A pocket watch she won from a conductor, which keeps railroad time
A letter from the owner of the Bonanza saloon at Plata Vieja engaging her to deal faro at $25 a week
features: Book Learning (Back East origin: reads and writes well and ciphers; advantage on Investigation checks to read documents, deeds, ledgers, telegrams and forged bills of sale; once per long rest recalls one useful fact about law, banking, railroads or the telegraph without a check)

Read the Table (Gambler: proficiency doubled for Gambling and Insight; once per short rest, after a minute of watching or talking to someone, learns one thing they are hiding; always knows whether a game is honest)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, +2d6 damage with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when she has advantage, when another enemy of the target is within 5 ft of it, or when the target believed a lie she told it in the last minute; not part of the damage on her sheet)
Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: 3 luck points per long rest; spend one to roll an extra d20 on an attack, check or save and choose, or to make a creature within 30 ft reroll an attack against her)

Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action unseen by anyone not watching her hands; advantage on Sleight of Hand to carry one past a search; can Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action)

Game: Faro Dealer (Gambler, 3rd level: in a town with a saloon she can set up a faro bank and earn 1d6 x 5 dollars a night, and the house always knows who is winning, who is drinking and who is broke)

Riding the Rails (Railroad Man background: four years a telegrapher on the Kansas lines and the River Line; reads Morse by ear at forty words a minute, so a sounder clicking in a depot is a conversation she can overhear; railroad crews, telegraphers and depot agents talk to her as one of their own; the River Line remembers her, and not kindly)

personality.traits: I listen to everything, including things that are not meant for me. I tap out what people say in Morse on the table without noticing. I am cheerful in a crisis and dreadful at breakfast.
personality.ideals: A telegram is a sealed letter. Whoever reads another person's message is a thief, however good his reasons, and I will not be one, even when I am tempted.
personality.bonds: The operators on every line I have worked, who are the only family I have. The memory of a wire I read in Albuquerque in June and should not have, and cannot forget.
personality.flaws: I lost my job for my principles and took up a trade with none. I like winning too much, and I like it best when I am winning against a man who thinks women cannot count.

appearance: A small, quick, sharp-featured woman of thirty with a cloud of fair hair pinned up anyhow, grey eyes, ink-stained fingers on her left hand and a laugh that carries. A mended green dress, a straw hat with a long pin through it, gloves she takes off to deal.
backstory: Theodora Quayle was born in 1851 in Providence, Rhode Island, the daughter of a railroad clerk who taught her Morse code for a parlour game, and at nineteen she was operating a key for the Kansas Pacific at a depot on the plains, where she found out that telegraphers know everything that happens in a town before the town does. She worked the Kansas lines for six years and came to Albuquerque in 1880 to operate for the River Line, and in May 1881 she was dismissed for insubordination. A Company man named Rusk had offered the night operator ten dollars a week for copies of other people's messages, and she reported it. The line chose Rusk. Before she left, she took down one Company wire she was never meant to see, on 20 June, from a printer on Railroad Avenue to Rusk at Paragon, and she remembers it word for word: ENVELOPES FOUR HUNDRED PRINTED AS ORDERED SHIP PARAGON FIRST WEEK JULY. She did not understand it, and still doesn't. With $60 and a faro box she is going to Plata Vieja on the Rio Seco line's last coach to deal at the Bonanza saloon, because it is as far from the railroad as she can get. (Suggested employer: the Southwestern Express Company's reward, or the miners; she has no love for the Company. Hooks: the wire of 20 June, the Paragon telegrapher who sells copies, and Rusk, whom she would know anywhere.)
